Difference-in-differences on the transmission scale: sequential moment estimation of policy effects on the reproduction number under feedback and spatial contagion

Apevon Science

Summary

Panels of reported cases are used to evaluate non-pharmaceutical interventions. Yet difference-in-differences estimators on case counts or log cases ignore three features of epidemic data. Transmission is multiplicative and self-exciting, policies are adopted in response to rising cases, and units infect each other. We propose a difference-in-differences design on the transmission scale, with parallel trends for the log reproduction number in a renewal model with infection pressure imported from neighbouring units and with policy spillover. A quasi-differenced generalized method of moments estimator removes unrestricted unit effects using only sequentially exogenous instruments. It is consistent for a fixed number of weeks when adoption depends on the past of all units, and cluster-robust inference remains valid under contagion between clusters. We derive the limits of two-step reproduction-number regressions and Poisson fixed-effects estimators. An estimator of cases averted carries the counterfactual through the renewal equation and the network. In a pre-specified simulation with contagion between units, the estimator had negligible bias and nominal coverage under adoption feedback, while standard estimators were biased or had inflated type I error. Without contagion the estimating equations had spurious roots, and we evaluate root-selection rules for this case. In an application to state mask orders and county COVID-19 cases in the United States, the estimated direct effect was imprecise, the working model was rejected, and event-time estimates were consistently negative.

Key words: Causal inference; Difference-in-differences; Generalized method of moments; Infectious disease epidemiology; Interference; Renewal equation.

1. Introduction

Panels of reported cases by county or region are the most common data for evaluating non-pharmaceutical interventions against an epidemic. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the effects of mask orders, stay-at-home orders and closures were estimated from such panels with event studies and two-way fixed-effects regressions of case growth or log cases (Lyu and Wehby, 2020; Hsiang et al., 2020; Guy et al., 2021; Chernozhukov et al., 2021). Other studies compared counties with and without an order (Van Dyke et al., 2020; Ginther and Zambrana, 2021) or used synthetic controls (Mitze et al., 2020). These designs borrow the difference-in-differences logic of policy evaluation (Roth et al., 2023; Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021). Epidemic data violate that logic in three ways that design reviews have stressed (Haber et al., 2021; Kennedy-Shaffer, 2024).

First, transmission is multiplicative and self-exciting. Cases in a week are generated by cases in earlier weeks through the generation interval (Wallinga, 2004; Fraser, 2007; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007), so parallel trends in case counts or log cases generally do not hold even without any policy (Gauthier, 2021; Feng and Bilinski, 2024). Second, adoption reacts to the epidemic. Governments impose orders when cases rise, so the policy depends on past outcomes. Unit fixed-effects estimators then lose their usual justification (Imai and Kim, 2019). The same problem is familiar from dynamic panels (Nickell, 1981). Third, units are coupled. Infections cross county borders and policies of neighbours change contact patterns, so the no-interference assumption fails (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Halloran and Hudgens, 2016; Aronow and Samii, 2017). Empirical work shows that ignoring such spillovers changes estimated policy effects (Enríquez et al., 2025). A further point concerns the estimand. The quantity of policy interest is often the number of cases averted, and an infection prevented in one week also prevents the infections it would have caused later and elsewhere.

Existing methods address parts of this problem. Feng and Bilinski (2024) place parallel trends on the log effective reproduction number. They estimate reproduction numbers first (Cori et al., 2013) and then regress them on the policy. Their approach is the closest in spirit to ours. Its authors note that spillovers are not considered, and estimated reproduction numbers inherit the small-count and generation-interval problems of the first step (Gostic et al., 2020). Semi-mechanistic renewal models estimate intervention effects on the reproduction number within a generative model, either in a Bayesian framework (Flaxman et al., 2020; Brauner et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2021; Bhatt et al., 2023) or with frequentist inference (Bong et al., 2025). Their identification comes from the model and from conditioning on the observed past (Bong et al., 2024), not from comparisons that remove unobserved unit levels. In a related line of work, Callaway and Li (2023) motivate an unconfoundedness assumption, conditional on lagged cases, with an SIR model. Similarly, Chernozhukov et al. (2021) use a structural causal model for growth rates. Neither approach removes time-invariant unit effects with a renewal structure. Count-data models with neighbourhood terms, such as the endemic–epidemic framework (Held et al., 2005; Meyer and Held, 2014; Lu and Meyer, 2023) and spatio-temporal Poisson autoregressions (Alaimo Di Loro et al., 2025), describe coupling between units. They are not designed for causal identification under feedback. In econometrics, quasi-differenced moment conditions remove multiplicative unit effects when regressors are only predetermined (Chamberlain, 1992; Wooldridge, 1997; Blundell et al., 2002). They have been used for a contagion-like count process outside epidemiology (Schweikert et al., 2021), but not with renewal pressure, network transmission or an epidemiological estimand. Nonlinear difference-in-differences for exponential means (Wooldridge, 2023) assumes strictly exogenous treatment. Finally, difference-in-differences with spillovers (Butts, 2021; Sun and Xiao, 2025) treats interference through exposure mappings on the outcome scale, without transmission dynamics or feedback from cases to adoption.

This paper proposes a difference-in-differences design on the transmission scale and an estimator for it. Parallel trends are assumed for the log reproduction number in a renewal model. In this model a unit’s infection pressure has a local part and a part imported from neighbours through a known network. The policy may act on the unit and on its neighbours. Adoption may depend on the entire past of all units, but not on current shocks. The contributions are as follows.

  1. A quasi-differenced generalised method of moments estimator (QD-GMM) that eliminates unit effects on the transmission scale and is consistent for a fixed number of weeks under adoption feedback, with closed-form profiling of week effects (Section 2.5).

  2. Identification and asymptotic theory under contagion between clusters (Theorems 1 and 2, Corollary 1). Moment contributions form a martingale difference array across weeks, so cluster-robust inference remains valid although neighbouring states exchange infections.

  3. Pseudo-true values of the standard estimators, which separate the small-count and feedback components of two-step estimates and show why Poisson fixed effects are inconsistent even with randomised adoption (Theorem 3). The constant-effect estimand puts non-negative weights on heterogeneous effects (Proposition 3).

  4. A cases-averted estimand in which an infection prevented in one week also removes the infections it would have caused later and in neighbouring units, with an estimator and inference for the realised-path quantity (Theorem 4).

  5. A simulation study, with design and success criteria fixed before it was run, that documents both the performance of the method and a failure mode. When there is no contagion between units, the estimating equations have spurious roots, and we evaluate root-selection procedures for this case.

Relative to the closest work, the differences are as follows. Compared with Feng and Bilinski (2024), the estimator works in one step on counts, without plug-in reproduction numbers, allows feedback with fixed T, and models contagion and policy spillover. Compared with Bong et al. (2025) and Bong et al. (2024), it keeps unrestricted unit effects that may be related to adoption and requires many clusters rather than long series. Compared with Callaway and Li (2023) and Chernozhukov et al. (2021), it replaces selection on observed lagged cases with parallel log-transmission trends. Compared with Wooldridge (1997) and Blundell et al. (2002), the mean has a renewal and network structure, the moments are shown to be uncorrelated across clusters despite transmission, and the estimand includes propagated cases averted. Compared with Butts (2021) and Sun and Xiao (2025), spillover enters through infection pressure and neighbours’ policies on the transmission scale, and treatment may respond to outcomes. We do not claim efficiency. The efficiency bound for sequential moment restrictions (Chamberlain, 1992; Chamberlain, 2022) is not derived, and moments that exploit a full Poisson likelihood (Bonhomme et al., 2025) are not used.

Section 2 sets out the model, assumptions, estimator and theory. Section 3 reports the simulation study, Section 4 an application to state mask orders and county COVID-19 cases in the United States in 2020, and Section 5 discusses limitations. Proofs and numerical checks are in Web Appendices A and B, and supplementary simulation results in Web Appendix C.

2. Methods

2.1 Setting, potential outcomes and estimands

Units i=1,…,N (counties) are partitioned into G clusters (states); g(i) denotes the cluster of unit i and the cluster sizes ng are bounded. Weeks are indexed by t=1−S,…,T; weeks 1,…,T form the estimation window and the S earlier weeks are used only to build lags. Yit denotes reported new cases and Dit∈{0,1} the policy, with Dit=0 for t≤0. The policy spillover κ is the corresponding effect of the share of neighbours under the policy, and the contagion coupling ϕ is the relative infectiousness of neighbours’ recent cases. 2.2 Assumptions

A1 (renewal model with parallel log-transmission trends).

For every policy array 𝐝, unit i and week t≥1, 𝔼{Yit(𝐝)∣α,Ht−1(𝐝)}=exp(αi+γt+τ0dit+κ0d¯it)Λit(𝐝;ϕ0).

A2 (no anticipation and sequential ignorability).

(a) Yit(𝐝) depends on 𝐝 only through 𝐝1,…,𝐝t. (b) For every t and 𝐝 with Pr(D1:t=𝐝1:t)>0, 𝔼{Yit(𝐝)∣α,Ht−1(𝐝),D1:t=𝐝1:t}=𝔼{Yit(𝐝)∣α,Ht−1(𝐝)}.

A3 (consistency).

Yit=Yit(D).

A4 (conditional independence across clusters).

For every t, conditionally on ℱt−1, the cluster vectors (Yit)i:g(i)=g, g=1,…,G, are independent.

A4′ (local dependence).

Let 𝒞 be the graph on clusters in which g and h are adjacent if Wij>0 for some i∈g, j∈h, or if the policy rule of g uses data from h; its maximal degree is bounded. (i) The cluster primitives (unit effects and pre-sample outcomes, weekly outcome innovations, weekly policy randomisation) are independent across clusters, and the week-t outcome innovations are independent of all primitives dated before week t and of the week-t policy randomisation. (ii) Dgt is a measurable function of the week-t policy randomisation of g and of the histories before week t of clusters within distance ρ of g in 𝒞; Ygt is a measurable function of the week-t innovation and unit effects of g and of the outcomes before week t and the week-t policies of g and of the clusters adjacent to g.

A5 (positive pressure).

Λit(ϕ)≥c>0 for all i, t and ϕ∈[0,ϕ¯].

A6 (regularity).

Web Appendix A.1: compact parameter space with θ0 interior; moment dominance; existence of the limits g¯, Γ, Ω defined below, with Ω positive definite; g¯(θ)=0 only at θ0; Γ of full rank.

A7 (reporting).

Reported cases are Yit=cictIit, where Iit are infections, ci>0 is a unit reporting factor and ct>0 a week reporting factor.

Assumption A1 states that, in the absence of any policy, logRit(0)=αi+γt. Untreated transmission paths are therefore parallel on the log scale, while levels may differ arbitrarily and may be related to adoption. The conditional variance is unrestricted, so overdispersion and clustering of cases are allowed. Assumption A2(b) is a mean version of sequential randomisation (Robins et al., 2000). Policies may depend on α and on the entire past of all units, which is the feedback that motivates this paper, but not on the shocks of the week they apply to. A4 allows arbitrary dependence within clusters and dependence across clusters through past outcomes (contagion); it rules out common unmodelled shocks to neighbouring clusters within a week beyond those absorbed by γt. A4′ implies A4 and is only used to verify the laws of large numbers. It fails when policies respond to national aggregates, in which case the laws of large numbers become high-level conditions. A5 holds by construction when ωi≥c.

Proposition 1 (Ascertainment). Suppose A1 holds for infections, with infection pressure ΛitI, and reported cases satisfy A7. Suppose also that the reported pressure uses the background term ωitY=cict−1ωiI and that either ϕ0=0 or ci=cj whenever Wij>0. (a) If ct−s=ct−1 for s=1,…,S, then reported cases satisfy A1 with the same αi, τ0, κ0, ϕ0 and with γt replaced by γt+log(ct/ct−1). (b) Otherwise, |logΛitY−log(cict−1ΛitI)|≤max1≤s≤S|log(ct−s/ct−1)|, so the error in the log reproduction number of week t is bounded by the largest relative change in ascertainment within the generation window.

Proposition 1 is why time-varying testing intensity does not bias τ as long as it is common across units and smooth relative to the generation interval. When reports are a binomial thinning of infections, the reported pressure is a noisy proxy for cict−1ΛitI, and A1 holds for reported data only approximately; we treat this case as a sensitivity analysis, not as a theorem.

Lemma 2 is the key to inference under contagion. Neighbouring clusters have correlated outcomes, because each one’s cases seed the other’s epidemic; this correlation is visible in the numerical checks of Web Appendix B. Their moment contributions are nevertheless uncorrelated, because each contribution is a sum of innovations weighted by predetermined quantities. The ordinary cluster-robust variance therefore remains valid and no spatial HAC correction is needed for θ̂.

Proposition 2 (Sources of identification). Assume A1–A3 and absorbing adoption. (a) If Dit=Di,t+1, then uit(θ) does not depend on τ. (b) The τ-column of Γ is

Treated stayers carry no direct information on τ; they enter only through the week effects, which are pinned down by all units. The effect is learned from the growth of cases in switchers relative to the common growth. Part (c) shows that the usual lead-placebo test is invalid under feedback. When adoption responds to high current cases, Cov(Di,t+1,εit∣ℱt−1)>0 and the lead moment is negative even though the model is correct. Leads are valid placebo instruments only when adoption dates are fixed at least two weeks in advance. Under feedback we instead test the model with the over-identification statistic of Corollary 1, using additional predetermined instruments.

Efficient two-step GMM with all available instruments is not our primary estimator. With G≈49 states and T+2 or more moments, the estimated optimal weight matrix is close to singular and two-step standard errors are known to be too small (Windmeijer, 2005). Over-identification is used only for specification tests with a few additional instruments.

The central-limit step uses a martingale argument over the T week blocks combined with a conditional Lindeberg argument across clusters within each block (Lemma 3, Web Appendix A). It is self-contained, so we need not appeal to the nesting conditions of the general martingale central limit theorem (Hall and Heyde, 1980). With independent clusters the result reduces to standard clustered-sample theory (Hansen and Lee, 2019). Instruments that depend on a first-step estimate, such as ϕ¯=ϕ̂ from a first pass or a predicted adoption hazard, do not change V (Lemma 5, Web Appendix A), because derivatives of predetermined instruments are orthogonal to uit(θ0).

Remark 1 (Working-optimal instruments). Ignoring the correlation between uit and ui,t+1 and using a Poisson working variance, 𝔼{∂uit/∂θ∣ℱt−1}=μit{−et,xit−𝔼(xi,t+1∣ℱt−1)} and var(uit∣ℱt−1)=μit{1+𝔼(rit∣ℱt−1)}, so the working-optimal instrument {xit−𝔼(xi,t+1∣ℱt−1)}/{1+𝔼(rit∣ℱt−1)} is free of αi. Its policy component is the predicted switching hazard, which can be estimated in a first step (Lemma 5). Fully efficient instruments for sequential moment restrictions require forward orthogonalisation (Chamberlain, 1992; Chamberlain, 2022), and we do not derive the efficiency bound. Under a full Poisson likelihood more feedback-robust moments exist (Bonhomme et al., 2025); under our conditional-mean model only quasi-differenced moments are used.

Part (a) separates two mechanisms. The Jensen term BJ is the small-count problem of estimated reproduction numbers and does not vanish as T grows. The feedback term BF arises because the unit mean of D uses future adoption, which responds to current shocks. This is the mechanism behind the fixed-T bias of within estimators in dynamic panels (Nickell, 1981). Our bound shows that BF decays no faster than T−1/2 in general. Part (b) shows that the Poisson fixed-effects estimator is inconsistent for fixed T even with randomised adoption, through the lagged-outcome offset. We do not derive a general O(1/T) rate. Split-panel jackknife corrections (Dhaene and Jochmans, 2015) assume stationarity, which week effects and staggered adoption violate, so the corrected estimator is assessed only by simulation.

2.7 Heterogeneous and dynamic effects

Proposition 3 (Heterogeneous effects). Suppose A1 holds with unit-specific, time-invariant τi, possibly dependent on αi and on the adoption process, adoption is absorbing, and (κ,ϕ)=(κ0,ϕ0) is fixed. Use the instruments of Theorem 1(b). Let Mt=limG−1𝔼∑isitμit and assume At>0, Kt>0 for some t. Then the pseudo-true value τ̃ exists, is unique, and lies in the closed convex hull of the support of τi under the measure sitμitSwi,t+1 restricted to weeks with At>0. A first-order expansion in τi−τ̃ gives the following approximation.

This is a weighted average with non-negative weights.

Unlike two-way fixed effects with staggered adoption (Goodman-Bacon, 2021; de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille, 2020), the constant-effect QD-GMM estimand cannot place negative weight on any unit’s effect when effects are time-invariant. Switchers in weeks with no treated units receive zero first-order weight.

Remark 2 (Dynamic effects). If the effect changes with time since adoption, treated stayers no longer cancel τ; their case growth contains τe+1−τe. Because already-treated units help pin down the week effects (Proposition 2), the constant-effect estimand can lie outside the range of the true effects and can even have the wrong sign, as with already-treated comparisons in two-way fixed effects (Goodman-Bacon, 2021). We therefore recommend the event-time specification ∑e=0Eτe1{t−Ai=e}, where Ai is the adoption week and the last bin collects e≥E, instrumented by sit1{t−Ai=e}. These indicators are ℱt−1-measurable, so Theorem 2 applies whenever the rank condition holds. The rank condition requires not-yet-treated or never-treated units.

2.8 Cases averted

Set νit=Yit for t≤0. For t≥1 the counterfactual is defined recursively, for all units jointly, as follows.

Here Λit(ν;ϕ) is the pressure computed from ν. The recursion leaves νit=Yit until a policy affects unit i directly, through D¯it, or through the pressure it receives, so no counterfactual start date has to be chosen. Let ψ̂𝒫=∑(i,t)∈𝒫{νit(θ̂)−Yit} and ψ𝒫†=∑(i,t)∈𝒫{νit(θ0)−Yit}.

Theorem 4 (Counterfactual propagation). (a) Under A1–A3 and A5, 𝔼(νit(θ0)∣α,Y≤0)=𝔼{Yit(0)∣α,Y≤0} for all i and t, so 𝔼ψ𝒫†=ψ𝒫. (b) Under the conditions of Theorem 2, if |𝒫|/G is bounded and the dominance conditions of Web Appendix A.1 hold for ∂νit/∂β, then G(ψ̂𝒫−ψ𝒫†)/G→dN(0,ΨVΨ⊤) with Ψ=plimG−1∑(i,t)∈𝒫∂νit(θ0)/∂θ⊤.

The naive rescaling Yite−τDit−κD¯it ignores that averted cases would themselves have infected others; Theorem 4 propagates the counterfactual through the renewal equation and the network. Inference in (b) targets the realised-path quantity ψ†, whose expectation is ψ.

Remark 3 (Process noise and depletion). ψ𝒫†−ψ𝒫 is a sum of mean-zero, locally dependent terms. Unlike the moment contributions, these terms are correlated across neighbouring clusters, because νit depends on neighbours’ outcomes. A variance estimator for the population-level ψ𝒫 would add a cluster-graph HAC term; we conjecture that it is consistent but do not prove it. If susceptible depletion multiplies the mean in A1 by 1−Ci,t−1/Pi, where C is cumulative cases and P population, the recursion is no longer linear in past ν and Theorem 4(a) holds only approximately.

Remark 4 (Testability). Lemma 2 implies that moment contributions of adjacent clusters are uncorrelated, which can be checked directly. The J test of Corollary 1 checks the multiplicative renewal structure against extra predetermined instruments. A sensitivity analysis lagging D by one week addresses anticipation. Sequential ignorability (A2(b)) and parallel untreated log-transmission paths after adoption are not testable.

2.9 Computation, variants and root selection

The primary estimator, M0, uses the instruments of Section 2.5 with the pre-specified reference value ϕ¯=0.5. It is computed by a local root search for β from a fixed starting value, with γ profiled out by (5). Three variants are used for checks and are fixed in advance. M0-OI adds two predetermined instruments, sitNi,t−1/Λi,t−1(ϕ¯) and sitlog{(Yi,t−1+0.5)/(Yi,t−2+0.5)}, and is estimated by two-step GMM; its role is to provide the J statistic of Corollary 1. M0-ET replaces τDit by event-time effects τ0,…,τ5 and a pooled effect for six or more weeks since adoption, as recommended in Remark 2. M0′ imposes κ=ϕ=0 and corresponds to Theorem 3(d).

Theorem 1 is a local result and A6 assumes that θ0 is interior. When contagion between units is absent (ϕ0=0), the true value is on the boundary of the parameter space. Estimating equations can then have several roots, of which at most one is consistent (Small et al., 2000), and boundary values change the limiting distribution of the estimator (Self and Liang, 1987; Andrews, 1999). We therefore pre-specified a global version, M0-G. For each ϕ on a grid in [0,3], (γ,τ,κ) are profiled out and the remaining ϕ-equation is evaluated. Every sign change on the grid is refined to a root, and the boundary point ϕ=0 is added as a candidate. Among the candidates, M0-G selects the one with the smallest over-identified GMM criterion Q computed with the M0-OI instruments, following the idea of choosing among roots with a goodness-of-fit criterion (Heyde, 1998). Inference is conditional on the selected candidate, and a boundary selection is reported as such, without a Wald interval for ϕ.

The simulation in Section 3 showed that this pre-specified rule is not sufficient. We therefore also report a variant designed after interim results had been seen, M0-GI, which is labelled post hoc wherever it appears. It uses the same candidates as M0-G, but Q is built from the M0 moments together with the ϕ-instrument evaluated at two other reference values, Nit/Λit(0.05) and Nit/Λit(2.0). The rationale follows from Lemma 1: moments formed with any predetermined instrument have mean zero at θ0, whatever the reference value, whereas a spurious root that solves the ϕ¯-instrument equation need not solve the equations at other reference values. Because the selection rule was chosen after seeing results, its performance requires confirmation in designs that were not used to choose it. The profiled ϕ-moment over the grid, together with Q, shows whether more than one root exists; both are reported for the application in Section 4.

3. Simulation Study

The design follows the ADEMP structure of Morris et al. (2019). Aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures and success criteria were written down before any full run. Departures from that protocol are listed at the end of the design description, before the results.

3.1 Design

3.1.1 Aims

The study had four aims. The first was to assess the finite-sample bias, standard errors and coverage of M0 for (τ,κ,ϕ) under adoption feedback, adoption related to unit effects, contagion, overdispersion and small counts (Theorem 2). The second was to assess inference for cases averted (Theorem 4), and the third to quantify the bias of the standard estimators and compare it with Theorem 3. The fourth was to assess the J test and the robustness of M0 when the working model is wrong.

3.1.2 Data-generating mechanisms

All scenarios use one generator. Counties are placed uniformly in the unit square and linked to their six nearest neighbours; the graph is symmetrised and W is its row-normalised adjacency matrix. Counties are grouped into G=50 spatially contiguous strips that play the role of states. Unit effects combine a state component, a county component and a term proportional to the state’s adoption propensity, so that adoption is related to transmission levels. Outcomes follow the mean (1) with S=2 lags, generation-interval weights (0.85,0.15), background input proportional to population, and negative binomial innovations with shape k=10, or Poisson innovations (k=∞). The week-effect level is calibrated so that median county-week counts lie between 5 and 50. Under random adoption, each state’s adoption week is uniform on {2,…,T+2}, so that some states remain untreated within the window. Under feedback adoption, a state adopts when its lagged incidence first exceeds a threshold that depends on its adoption propensity, and a county of an adopting state starts when its own lagged incidence exceeds a second threshold. Adoption is absorbing.

The 25 scenarios form three blocks. The core block crosses N∈{500,2000}, T∈{12,26}, random or feedback adoption, and spillover (ϕ0,κ0)=(0.4,−0.1) or none, (0,0), with τ0=log0.8 (scenarios 1–16). The null block (scenarios 17–20) sets τ0=0, N=500, T=12 with spillover, and crosses the adoption rule with k∈{10,∞}. The misspecification block (scenarios 21–25) uses N=2000, T=26, feedback adoption and spillover, and violates one assumption at a time. In X1 the true generation interval is (0.7,0.3) but (0.85,0.15) is used. In X2 reports are a binomial thinning of infections with a reporting probability that falls by 15% after the state adopts. In X3 the effects are unit-specific, τi∼N(log0.8,0.12). In X4 the mean is multiplied by the susceptible fraction, with cumulative attack rates up to about 20%. In X5 effects grow with time since adoption from −0.1 to −0.3.

3.1.3 Estimands

The targets are the generating values of τ, κ and ϕ. In X3 the target of τ is also compared with the replication-specific mean of τi among switchers and with the first-order pseudo-true value of Proposition 3; in X5 the targets are the event-time effects. For cases averted, the inferential target in each replication is ψ†, computed from the recursion (7) at the true parameter for the treated unit-weeks and for all unit-weeks after adoption (network). The population quantity ψ of (2) is approximated in each scenario from 5000 pairs of policy and no-policy paths generated with common random numbers.

3.1.4 Methods

All methods are applied to the same data sets. The proposed estimator M0 is run together with its variants M0-G, M0-GI (post hoc), M0-OI, M0-ET and M0′ (Section 2.9). M1 is Poisson fixed effects with offset logΛit(ϕ) and free (κ,ϕ) (Hausman et al., 1984; Wooldridge, 1999), and M1-BC is its split-panel jackknife correction (Dhaene and Jochmans, 2015; Fernández-Val and Weidner, 2016). M2 is the two-step log-R difference-in-differences of Theorem 3(a), with weekly reproduction numbers estimated by the method of Cori et al. (2013). M3 is two-way fixed effects on log(Y+1), and M4 is pooled renewal Poisson quasi-likelihood without unit effects. The infeasible Oracle is Poisson quasi-likelihood with the true unit effects. All intervals are cluster-robust with tG−1 critical values. Failures are recorded per method and are not replaced.

3.1.5 Performance measures

For each scenario and method we computed bias, empirical standard error, mean model standard error and its relative error, and root mean squared error. We also computed coverage of nominal 95% intervals, the rejection rates of H0:τ=0 at the 5% level and of the J test, and the convergence rate. Each measure is reported with its Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). Each scenario used R=8000 replications with seeds that depend on the scenario and replication number.

3.1.6 Pre-specified criteria

M0 was to be considered supported if, in the feedback scenarios, its bias for τ, κ and ϕ was within 2 MCSE of zero and its coverage was in [93%,97%], while M2 and M3 had biases larger than 2 MCSE or coverage below 90%. If M1 and M1-BC had negligible bias and correct coverage in every feedback scenario, the contribution would be limited to the transmission-scale framework, spillover parameters, inference under contagion and cases averted.

3.1.7 Departures from the protocol

The spread of the unit effects was reduced by a factor of 4, because with the protocol values counts at T=26 became unrealistically large. The number of replications was raised from 1000 to 8000, the largest value allowed by the computing budget. M0-G was added after a small pilot showed multiple roots, before any full run. M0-GI was added after interim results showed that M0 and M0-G under-covered in every scenario without spillover. It is therefore reported separately and labelled post hoc. Finally, the optional estimator with working-optimal instruments (Remark 1) and a group-time average treatment effect estimator (Callaway and Sant’Anna, 2021) were not run.

3.2 Results

3.2.1 Contagion present

Table 1 and Figure 1 show the results for τ in the core scenarios. In the eight scenarios with spillover, M0 had bias between −0.002 and 0.001 and coverage between 94.5% and 95.4%, under both random and feedback adoption. Model standard errors matched the empirical standard errors, and their relative error lay between −3.5% and 0.9% across τ, κ and ϕ in all scenarios with spillover in the core and null blocks (for τ, see Web Table 1). Power against τ0=log0.8 was between 77.1% and 100%. The spillover parameters were also recovered (Web Table 2 and Web Figures 1 and 2). With R=8000, the strict criterion |bias|≤2 MCSE detects very small biases. For τ it failed only in scenario 1 (bias −0.0017, 2.18 MCSE); for κ only in scenario 9 (2.26 MCSE). For ϕ it failed in scenarios 1, 2, 3, 9, 10 and 17–20, with the largest bias 0.0035 (5.43 MCSE, scenario 9). Coverage for all three parameters was within the pre-specified interval. The finite-sample bias of ϕ̂ is therefore small but detectable, and the criterion is met only in a qualified sense.

The standard estimators did not meet the criterion. In the spillover scenarios, M1 had bias between −0.027 and −0.017 and coverage between 78.1% and 88.2%, under random as well as feedback adoption, as Theorem 3(b) predicts. The split-panel correction M1-BC did not remove the problem. It converged in only 14.7% and 23.9% of replications in scenarios 2 and 4, and its coverage ranged from 25.7% to 82.7%. M2 had bias between −0.110 and 0.013, M3 between −0.563 and −0.030, and M4 between 0.008 and 0.139. Ignoring spillover (M0′) gave bias between −0.248 and −0.114 and coverage of at most 22.4%, in line with Theorem 3(d). The Oracle, which knows the unit effects, had coverage between 91.3% and 94.8%. The condition for limiting the contribution was not met.

3.2.2 Type I error

Under the null (Web Table 3 and Web Figure 3), M0 rejected in 4.7% to 5.2% of replications, M0-OI in 5.7% to 6.4% and the first event-time bin of M0-ET in 3.9% to 4.9%. M1 rejected in 6.3% to 9.7%, M1-BC in 14.7% to 28.6%, M2 in 76.1% to 100% and M3 in 11.9% to 61.9%. M4 ranged from 4.6% to 100%, depending on the adoption rule. The J test of M0-OI had size between 4.4% and 4.9%.

3.2.3 No contagion and multiple roots

When ϕ0=κ0=0, the true value lies on the boundary of the parameter space and the pre-specified estimator failed (Tables 1 and 2). For τ, the bias of M0 ranged from 0.132 to 0.469 and its coverage from 0.6% to 38.8%; the bias of ϕ̂ was between 0.232 and 0.888 and that of κ̂ between −0.457 and −0.150. The root diagnostics explain the failure (Figure 2 and Web Table 4). In 47.2% to 51.7% of replications the profiled equations had more than one interior root, and the local solver often settled on a spurious one. A diagnostic run showed that the spurious root moves with the reference value ϕ¯ of the ϕ-instrument. The J test detected the problem only in 6.4% to 27.2% of replications. The pre-specified global search M0-G reduced the bias to between 0.039 and 0.202 but left coverage between 52.9% and 71.0%; it chose the boundary in 28.6% to 44.8% of replications. The post hoc selection rule M0-GI chose the boundary in 63.7% to 80.9% of replications; its bias ranged from 0.000 to 0.052 and its coverage from 87.5% to 95.2%. Its worst case was the smallest design with random adoption (N=500, T=12, scenario 13). In the core and null scenarios with spillover, M0-G selected the same root as M0 in every replication, and M0-GI gave the same summaries as M0. In this block M0′ is correctly specified, and its bias stayed within [−0.000,0.002] with coverage of 94.7% to 95.5%. M1 showed biases from −0.048 to −0.008 with 51.3% to 91.1% coverage, and the Oracle had coverage between 80.2% and 94.5%.

3.2.4 Misspecification

Web Table 5 and Web Figure 4 report the misspecification block. With a wrong generation interval (X1), the bias of τ̂ was 0.010 with coverage 94.6%; the error was absorbed mainly by ϕ̂ (bias 0.516), and the J test rejected in 100% of replications. When reporting fell after adoption (X2), τ̂ had bias −0.057 and coverage 59.4%, κ̂ had bias −0.294, and J again rejected in every replication; M1 (−0.099) and M2 (−0.094) were more biased. With heterogeneous effects (X3), the bias of τ̂ was 0.005, both against the switcher mean and against the first-order value of Proposition 3, with coverage 94.0%. Susceptible depletion (X4) left τ̂ unbiased (bias −0.000, coverage 95.2%). With dynamic effects (X5), the constant-effect estimator had bias 0.219 relative to τ0=log0.8 and coverage 0%, so that its mean lay outside the range of the true event-time effects, as Remark 2 warns. The J test had no power against this departure (4.7%), but the event-time specification M0-ET recovered every event-time effect (bias −0.000, coverage 95.3% to 95.8%).

3.2.5 Cases averted

Web Table 6 reports ψ̂ for the treated unit-weeks. With spillover, the median relative bias was between −0.004 and 0.006, and coverage of ψ† ranged from 85.7% to 95.4%; it was below 93% in scenarios 1, 2, 4 and 10 (92.4%, 85.7%, 91.9% and 90.1%). The three largest shortfalls occurred with T=26, where the recursion compounds over more weeks. Coverage of the population quantity ψ was lower, between 72.1% and 92.5%, as expected from Remark 3. Without spillover, ψ̂ inherited the bias of M0, with median relative bias up to 2.474 (scenario 14). Under misspecification the median relative bias was 3.386 (X1), 1004.524 (X2, coverage 50.8%), 0.779 (X3) and −0.994 (X5, coverage 0%); under depletion (X4) coverage of the population ψ fell to 53.5%. Cases averted are thus far more sensitive to misspecification than τ.

4. Application: State Mask Orders and County COVID-19 Transmission

4.1 Data and specification

We illustrate the method with public mask orders in the United States in the second half of 2020. The effect of these orders on case growth has been studied with state and county panels (Lyu and Wehby, 2020; Guy et al., 2021; Van Dyke et al., 2020; Chernozhukov et al., 2021; Sun and Xiao, 2025). The design is a county panel of weekly reported cases. The analysis was specified before estimation, and we report it following the relevant items of the STROBE checklist for observational studies.

4.1.1 Setting and units

The estimation window has 26 weeks, from the week starting 2020-06-01 to the week starting 2020-11-23, with two earlier weeks used only to build lags. Units are the 3091 counties, or merged county reporting units, of the contiguous United States and the District of Columbia, grouped into 49 clusters, namely the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Alaska, Hawaii and the territories are excluded.

4.1.2 Outcome and exposure

The outcome Yit is the weekly number of newly reported confirmed cases, the difference of cumulative counts from the Johns Hopkins University CSSE repository (Dong et al., 2020), with negative revisions truncated at zero. The exposure Dit equals 1 if a state or territorial public mask order was in force on at least four of the seven days of the week, according to the county-by-day dataset of the Public Health Law Program of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021). County opt-outs that were permitted under state law, notably in Kansas, are not coded in that dataset, so D overstates exposure in such states. The exposure is not strictly absorbing; the estimator does not require it to be.

4.1.3 Network, generation interval and background input

The main network is the row-normalised 2010 Census county adjacency matrix; a sensitivity analysis uses county-to-county commuting flows from the American Community Survey 2011–2015. Weekly renewal weights are obtained by discretising the generation-time distribution of Ferretti et al. (2020) under a uniform infection day within the week, keeping lags 1 and 2. This gives w≈(0.964,0.036); the same-week mass of about 0.30 cannot be represented in a weekly lagged model. A sensitivity analysis uses the serial interval of Nishiura et al. (2020), giving w≈(0.913,0.087), and a grid of values of the lag-1 weight w1∈{0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0} with w2=1−w1. The background input is ωi = population/105.

4.1.4 Statistical methods

The main analysis is M0 with ϕ¯=0.5, inference clustered by state with t48 critical values (2.0106). We also report M0-G, the post hoc M0-GI, M0-OI with its J test, M0-ET, M0′ and the comparators M1–M4 of Section 3. The pre-specified sensitivity analyses vary the generation interval, the network, the timing of the policy (lagged by one week, addressing anticipation), the background input (ω×0.25 and ω×4) and the reference value ϕ¯, and exclude Kansas and Texas, whose orders had county exemptions. A conventional lead-indicator regression is reported for comparison only, because under adoption feedback the lead moment is not zero even when the model is correct (Proposition 2(c)). Cases averted are reported cumulatively over the first h∈{4,8,13,26} weeks, summed over all counties.

4.2 Results

4.2.1 Descriptive data

The median weekly count was 27 cases per county and the mean 143.446; 7.4% of county-weeks had no reported case. A mask order was in force in 56.8% of county-weeks. 2291 units were exposed at some time in the window, 571 at its start, and 1768 units changed exposure status within the window. The analysis units reported 11528182 cases in the window.

4.2.2 Main estimates

Table 3 and Figure 3 summarise the estimates. M0 gave τ̂=0.040 (95% confidence interval −0.217 to 0.296) for a county’s own order, κ̂=−0.506 (−1.018 to 0.006) for the share of neighbours under an order, and ϕ̂=0.772 (0.590 to 0.954) for the weight of imported infection pressure. The profiled ϕ-moment had a single zero crossing on the grid (Figure 3(b)), so M0-G and M0-GI selected the same root as M0. The estimate of ϕ is far from the boundary, the case in which the simulation supports M0. The data thus do not show an effect of a county’s own order on its reproduction number, and are compatible with a reduction of transmission when neighbouring counties are under an order, although the interval for κ includes zero.

The over-identification test rejected the working model (J=17.873, 2 degrees of freedom, p=0.0001). M0-OI, which uses the additional instruments, gave τ̂=−0.025 (−0.249 to 0.199) and κ̂=−0.517 (−0.983 to −0.050). The event-time specification M0-ET gave negative estimates in every bin, from −0.232 (standard error 0.269) in the week of adoption to −0.577 (0.493) five weeks later and −0.557 (0.546) for six or more weeks; the joint Wald test that all seven bins are zero gave F=2.642 on 7 and 42 degrees of freedom (p=0.0234). The average of the first six bins, which was not pre-specified and is descriptive, was −0.412 (−1.154 to 0.330). The constant-effect estimate near zero and the negative event-time profile are the pattern that Remark 2 and scenario X5 associate with effects that grow after adoption. They are also compatible with a change in ascertainment after adoption, which in scenario X2 the J test detected. The data cannot separate these explanations. The lead regression gave −0.332 (standard error 0.259, t=−1.283).

The comparators gave τ̂ between −0.084 (M2) and 0.087 (M3). M1 gave −0.024 (−0.109 to 0.061) with a much smaller κ̂ than M0, and the pooled model M4 estimated almost no contagion between counties (ϕ̂=0.027). Imposing κ=ϕ=0 (M0′) gave an interval from −2.088 to 2.130.

4.2.3 Sensitivity analyses

Across the pre-specified sensitivity analyses, τ̂ from M0 ranged from −0.177 (policy lagged one week) to 0.120 (w1=1.0), and every interval contained zero. The estimate of ϕ depended strongly on the generation interval, from 0.198 at w1=0.6 to 0.971 at w1=1.0, and on the network (0.240 with commuting flows). Excluding Kansas and Texas (2732 units in 47 clusters) gave τ̂=−0.035 (−0.285 to 0.214). The pre-specified global search M0-G departed from M0 in five analyses. It selected the boundary ϕ=0 with the policy lagged one week (τ̂=−2.178) and with ω×4 (τ̂=−1.274), and roots with ϕ̂≤0.010 for w1∈{0.6,0.7,0.9}, with wide intervals for τ. The post hoc M0-GI selected the M0 root in every analysis.

4.2.4 Cases averted

The estimated number of cases averted grew rapidly with the horizon. It was 3.41×105 (standard error 3.97×105) over the first 4 weeks, 5.62×106 (1.03×107) over 8 weeks, 5.61×107 (1.66×108) over 13 weeks and 7.17×1010 (5.16×1011) over 26 weeks, against 7.67×106 observed cases in treated county-weeks. The 26-week value exceeds the population of the country. It results from compounding the estimated neighbour effect through the renewal equation and the network without susceptible depletion (Remark 3). Only the short-horizon estimates are interpretable, and even these have standard errors as large as the estimates.

5. Discussion

For panels of reported cases we have proposed parallel trends in log transmission, together with a quasi-differenced GMM estimator that removes unit effects without requiring strictly exogenous adoption, and an estimator of cases averted based on the counterfactual renewal recursion. When contagion between units is present, the simulation study supports the method under adoption feedback, overdispersion and small counts, and shows that the commonly used alternatives are biased or have incorrect size. It also shows a failure mode that we did not anticipate in the protocol.

The results lead to three recommendations for practice. Because the estimating equations can have several roots and a local solver gives no warning, an estimate from M0 should be reported together with the profiled ϕ-moment and the selection criterion Q over a grid of ϕ (Figure 3(b)). The over-identification test of M0-OI should also be reported. In the spirit of specification tests for sequential moment conditions in dynamic panels (Arellano and Bond, 1991), it detected a wrong generation interval and a change in ascertainment after adoption in every replication, although it had little power against a wrong root and none against effects that build up over time. When effects may grow with time since adoption, the event-time specification M0-ET should be the primary analysis. In scenario X5 the constant-effect estimate fell outside the range of the true effects, while M0-ET recovered them. This parallels the problems of constant-effect regressions in event studies with heterogeneous effects (Sun and Abraham, 2021; Borusyak et al., 2024). The constant effect does retain an interpretation as a non-negatively weighted average when effects vary across units (Proposition 3), which scenario X3 confirmed. More generally, the results support estimating the multiplicative mean directly rather than a regression on log-transformed counts, whose estimates depend on how zeros are handled (Silva and Tenreyro, 2006; Chen and Roth, 2024); on the null scenarios M3 rejected in up to 61.9% of replications.

The main limitation of the method is its behaviour when the true ϕ is at or near zero. The neighbour term then carries no identifying information, the parameter lies on the boundary of its space (Self and Liang, 1987; Andrews, 1999), and the just-identified equations have spurious interior roots in about half of the replications. The estimator with ϕ fixed at zero (M0′) had nominal coverage in exactly these scenarios, which indicates that the failure is one of global identification of the estimating equations rather than of the moment conditions themselves. The pre-specified global search M0-G reduced the bias but not the under-coverage. The rule M0-GI, which adds moments that are informative about ϕ near zero, chose the right root in most replications, but it was designed after interim results were available and its properties were evaluated on the same designs that motivated it. In the smallest design with random adoption its coverage was still 87.5%. M0-GI therefore needs validation on new designs before it can replace M0-G, and a selection rule with guaranteed properties remains to be found (Small et al., 2000; Heyde, 1998). Near the boundary, identification of ϕ and κ is weak, and conventional Wald intervals may be unreliable even at the correct root. Inference that is robust to weak identification (Stock and Wright, 2000; Andrews et al., 2019) is a natural extension. In the application, the estimate of ϕ was far from zero and all selection rules agreed in the main analysis, but M0-G moved to near-boundary roots in five of the sensitivity analyses, so the issue is not only theoretical.

The estimate of ϕ has a small finite-sample bias, at most 0.0035 in the simulation, that the strict 2-MCSE criterion detects with 8000 replications. It did not affect coverage. The interval for cases averted under-covered for the realised-path target in some scenarios with T=26, as low as 85.7%. A plausible explanation is that the delta method is inaccurate for products of counterfactual factors compounded over many weeks; resampling or profile-based intervals may perform better.

Identification rests on parallel trends in log transmission and on sequential exogeneity of adoption given the observed past. The latter cannot be tested from the moments used for estimation (Remark 4), and the conventional lead placebo is not a valid check under adoption feedback (Proposition 2(c)); pre-tests of parallel trends also distort subsequent inference (Roth, 2022). Sensitivity analysis for violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth, 2023) could be adapted to the transmission scale. The model treats the generation interval and the network as known. The estimate of τ was robust to a wrong generation interval in scenario X1, but ϕ absorbed the error, and in the application the estimate of ϕ ranged from 0.198 to 0.971 across the generation intervals considered. Changes in ascertainment that coincide with adoption are not identified separately from transmission effects (scenario X2). A transmission signal that is less dependent on testing, such as wastewater concentrations (Goldstein et al., 2023), or a model for reporting delays (Lison et al., 2024), would be needed to separate them. The model also ignores susceptible depletion. With attack rates up to about 20% this did not bias τ (scenario X4), but it reduced the coverage of the population cases-averted target to 53.5%, and depletion is a known source of spurious time-varying effects in infectious-disease studies (Janvin and Stensrud, 2025). Including the susceptible fraction in the mean would be required for long horizons or high attack rates.

The simulation used one family of data-generating mechanisms, with two generation-interval lags, a nearest-neighbour graph, 50 clusters and one type of adoption rule. Behaviour with few clusters, for which small-sample corrections of cluster-robust inference matter (Imbens and Kolesár, 2016), with longer generation intervals or with other network shapes was not studied. In the application the over-identification test rejected the working model, so the estimates should be read as conditional on a model that is at least partly misspecified. The negative event-time profile is consistent with effects that build up after adoption and also with a change in ascertainment; the data do not distinguish these explanations, and the cases-averted estimates are not informative beyond a few weeks.

One natural extension is a set of instruments that attain the efficiency bound for sequential moment restrictions (Chamberlain, 1992; Chamberlain, 2022) or that exploit the full count likelihood (Bonhomme et al., 2025). Others are group-time and dynamic causal effects defined on the transmission scale (Bojinov et al., 2021); generation intervals and reporting processes estimated jointly with the policy effect, building on frequentist renewal estimators (Goldwasser et al., 2026); and a bias correction for ϕ̂.

Data Availability Statement

All data used in the application are publicly available. Weekly case counts were derived from the Johns Hopkins University CSSE COVID-19 repository (Dong et al., 2020) and mask orders from the CDC Public Health Law Program (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021). The county adjacency file and county-to-county commuting flows are from the US Census Bureau. Code that downloads the data, verifies file checksums, reproduces the simulation study and the application, and regenerates every table and figure is provided as part of the reproducibility package accompanying this article.

Lemma 3 (Local law of large numbers). Assume A4′ and let L=(ρ+1)(T+1)+1. If fg is a measurable function of the primitives of the clusters within distance L of g in 𝒞 and supg𝔼∥fg∥2≤C, then G−1∑g(fg−𝔼fg)→p0. Each of the variables listed in (L) is of this form, so A4′ and A6(ii)–(iii) imply (L).

Proof. [Proof of Theorem 1] (a) 𝔼{zituit(θ0)}=𝔼{zit𝔼(uit∣ℱt−1)}=0 by Lemma 1, so g¯(θ0)=0. If the rank is constant at r<p near θ0, the constant-rank theorem shows that {θ:g¯(θ)=0} contains a manifold of dimension p−r through θ0, so θ0 is not locally identified; this is the moment analogue of Theorem 1 of Rothenberg (1971).

A.5 Proofs for Section 2.5

Proof. [Proof of Theorem 2] (a) Let Q̂(θ)=ĝ(θ)⊤Ŵĝ(θ) and Q(θ)=g¯(θ)⊤Wg¯(θ). By (L), ĝ(θ)−g¯(θ)→p0 for each θ. Also ∥ĝ(θ)−ĝ(θ′)∥≤BG∥θ−θ′∥ with BG=G−1∑gsupθ∥∂gg/∂θ⊤∥=Op(1) by A6(ii) and Markov’s inequality. Corollary 2.2 of Newey (1991) gives supΘ∥ĝ−g¯∥→p0, so supΘ|Q̂−Q|→p0. Q is continuous and uniquely minimised at θ0 (A6(iv)), and Theorem 2.1 of Newey and McFadden (1994) gives θ̂→pθ0. In the just-identified case, θ̂ is the root with Q̂(θ̂)=0, which exists with probability tending to one by the argument in (b).

(b) Because θ0 is interior, with probability tending to one Γ̂(θ̂)⊤Ŵĝ(θ̂)=0, where Γ̂(θ)=∂ĝ(θ)/∂θ⊤. A row-wise mean-value expansion gives ĝ(θ̂)=ĝ(θ0)+Γ̂(θ¯)(θ̂−θ0). By the second-derivative envelope in A6(ii), (L) and the same uniform argument, supΘ∥Γ̂(θ)−Γ¯(θ)∥→p0, so Γ̂(θ̂) and Γ̂(θ¯) both converge to Γ. Hence G(θ̂−θ0)=−(Γ⊤WΓ)−1Γ⊤WGĝ(θ0)+op(1). By Lemma 2, Gĝ(θ0)=G−1/2∑g∑sξgs, with ξgs conditionally independent across clusters given ℱs−1 by A4. Lemma 4, with the conditions verified in A.1, gives Gĝ(θ0)→dN(0,Ω) with Ω=∑sΣs=limG−1∑g𝔼(gggg⊤) (Lemma 2). The influence-function representation and V follow.

(c) Γ̂(θ̂)→pΓ was shown in (b). Write dg=supθ∥∂gg/∂θ⊤∥. Then

because the averages are Op(1) by Cauchy–Schwarz and A6(ii). By (L) and Lemma 2, G−1∑ggg(θ0)gg(θ0)⊤→pΩ. The cross products gggh⊤, g≠h, are excluded from Ω̂, and this is justified because their means are zero (Lemma 2); the dependence between clusters affects only the rate of the law of large numbers, which Lemma 3 controls. The factor G/(G−1) tends to one. ∎

A.6 Proofs for Section 2.6

Proof. [Proof of Theorem 3] (a) With κ0=ϕ0=0, logμit=αi+γt+τ0Dit+logΛit. So yit=αi+γt+τ0Dit−bit+ηit identically. Two-way demeaning in a balanced panel removes αi and γt, which gives the exact identity. For the limit, decompose D̈it=Dit−D¯i⋅−D¯⋅t+D¯⋅⋅. The terms ∑Ditηit and ∑tD¯⋅t∑iηit have mean zero because Dit and D¯⋅t are ℱt−1-measurable, and divided by N they are op(1) by (L). The same holds for D¯⋅⋅∑ηit, since |D¯⋅⋅|≤1 and N−1∑ηit→p0. Finally ∑iD¯i⋅∑tηit=T−1∑i∑s,tDisηit, where the terms with t≥s have mean zero because Dis is ℱs−1-measurable. Hence N−1∑D̈itηit→p−T−1limN−1𝔼∑i∑t<sDisηit. Together with N−1∑D̈itbit→plimN−1𝔼∑D̈itbit and N−1∑D̈it2→pd2 (both by (L)), this gives BJ+BF.

For the bound, Mi,s−1=∑t<sηit is a martingale with 𝔼Mi,s−12≤(s−1)σ¯η2, and |Dis|≤1. Hence |𝔼∑t<sDisηit|=|𝔼DisMi,s−1|≤σ¯η(s−1)1/2, and comparing the sum with the integral of x1/2 over [0,T] gives ∑s=1T(s−1)1/2≤2T3/2/3. If instead ∑s∑t<s|𝔼Disηit|≤CT (adoption responds mainly to recent shocks), then |BF|≤C/d2. The expansion of bit is a second-order delta-method approximation. With var(Yit∣ℱt−1)=μit+μit2/k, 𝔼{log(Yit+c)∣ℱt−1}≈log(μit+c)−var/{2(μit+c)2}. Expanding in 1/μit gives logμit+(c−1/2+c/k)/μit−1/(2k)+O(μit−2), which was checked symbolically (Web Appendix B, S4). The constant −1/(2k) is absorbed by the fixed effects.

(b) The Poisson fixed-effects score for unit i, after concentrating out αi, is ∑sxis{Yis−mis∑rYir/∑rmir}=∑s(xis−x¯im)Yis. At β0, ∑s(xis−x¯im)μis=eαi{∑sxismis−x¯im∑smis}=0. Also 𝔼(xisεis)=0 because xis is ℱs−1-measurable, which leaves −∑s𝔼(x¯imεis). The Chen–Stein identity 𝔼{(Y−μ)f(Y)}=μ𝔼{f(Y+1)−f(Y)} for Y∼Poisson(μ) (Chen, 1975), applied conditionally on ℱs−1 and Ris, gives the representation. For T=2, conditioning on Yi1+Yi2 shows that the score for the week-2 effect of group d is ∑i1(Di2=d)(Yi2Λi1−Yi1ehΛi2)/(Λi1+ehΛi2). Taking the conditional expectation of Yi2 given ℱ1, which contains Yi1, Λi2 and Di2, yields (6). At h=h0+τ0d, the left side of (6) equals −eh𝔼[1(Di2=d)Cov{fh(Yi1),Yi1∣αi,Λi1,Di2}] with fh(y)=(y+ωi)/{Λi1+eh(y+ωi)} strictly increasing, which is strictly negative when Yi1 is non-degenerate. Under randomisation Di2 is independent of Yi1, but fh depends on h, so the two group-specific distortions differ.

(c) log(Yit+1)=αi+γt+τ0Dit+logΛit−bit(1)+ηit(1); apply two-way demeaning as in (a).

(d) Write Λit0=Lit+ωi. With κ=ϕ=0, uit(δ,τ)=Yi,t+1e−δt+τ(Dit−Di,t+1)Λit0/Λi,t+10−Yit. Taking 𝔼(⋅∣ℱt) and using A1 at θ0, 𝔼(Yi,t+1∣ℱt)e−δt+τ(Dit−Di,t+1)Λit0/Λi,t+10=μitRit(δ,τ) with Λit(ϕ0)/Λit0=1+ϕ0Ñit. Then 𝔼(zituit)=𝔼{zitμit(Rit−1)} because 𝔼(Yit∣ℱt−1)=μit. At κ0=ϕ0=0, (δ0,τ0) solves the equations. Linearising R−1≈logR around this point gives the weighted, just-identified instrumental-variable normal equations for the regression of κ0ΔD¯+ϕ0ΔÑ on week indicators and ΔD. The implicit function theorem then makes τ̃−τ0 equal to that coefficient up to O(κ02+ϕ02). ∎

A.7 Proof of Proposition 3

Proof. Include τi in the unit heterogeneity, so that ℱt contains (αi,τi); Lemma 1 then holds with μit=eαi+γt+τiDit+κ0D¯itΛit(ϕ0). As in the proof of Theorem 1(b), h(τ)=−∑tAtCt(τ)/{Mt+Ct(τ)} with Ct(τ)=limG−1𝔼∑isitμitSwi,t+1(eτi−τ−1), which is strictly decreasing in τ when Kt>0. Hence h is strictly increasing. If τ is below every τi in the stated support, all Ct>0 and h<0; if it is above, all Ct<0 and h>0. Note that Mt+Ct>0 because treated units and switchers are disjoint, so At≤Mt−Kt. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem give a unique root inside the convex hull. To first order, Ct(τ)≈Ht−τKt with Ht=limG−1𝔼∑isitμitSwi,t+1τi, and Ct/(Mt+Ct)≈Ct/Mt. Solving ∑t(At/Mt)(Ht−τKt)=0 gives the stated weighted average, with weights (At/Mt)sitμitSwi,t+1≥0. ∎

A.8 Proof of Theorem 4

Proof. (a) Let mit0=𝔼{Yit(0)∣α,Y≤0}. Pre-sample outcomes do not depend on the policy (A2(a)), so mit0=Yit for t≤0. For t≥1, A1 with 𝐝=0 and the tower property give mit0=eαi+γt{∑swsmi,t−s0+ϕ0∑sws∑jWijmj,t−s0+ωi}. For ν, cit(θ0) is ℱt−1-measurable and well defined by A5, so Lemma 1 gives 𝔼(νit∣ℱt−1)=citμit=eαi+γtΛit(ν;ϕ0). Because Λit(ν;ϕ0) is affine in past ν and σ(α,Y≤0)⊆ℱt−1, the conditional means 𝔼(νit∣α,Y≤0) satisfy the same recursion with the same initial values. Induction on t gives equality, and summing over 𝒫 gives 𝔼ψ𝒫†=ψ𝒫.

(b) νit(θ) depends on θ only through β and is continuously differentiable. By the mean-value theorem, (ψ̂𝒫−ψ𝒫†)/G={G−1∑𝒫∂νit(θ¯)/∂θ⊤}(θ̂−θ0). The bracket converges in probability to Ψ by the assumed dominance, (L) and the consistency of θ̂. The result follows from Theorem 2(b) and Slutsky’s lemma. ∎

Web Appendix B: Numerical checks

The script numeric_checks.py (supplementary code) verifies each derivation; seeds are fixed. All symbolic checks pass. They cover the quasi-difference identity of Lemma 2 (S1), the Jacobian (4) (S2), the closed-form profiling (5) (S3), the expansion of bit (S4), the identity rit2μi,t+1=ritμit behind the working variance in Remark 1 (S5), the first-order heterogeneity weights (S7), and the T=2 expected score (6) (S8). The expansion of bit is accurate for μit≥5; at μit=2, k=10, c=0.5 the exact value of 𝔼log(Y+c)−logμ is −0.00556 against −0.025 from the expansion.

The Monte Carlo check of Theorem 2 used R=1000 replications, T=10, τ0=log0.8, κ0=−0.1, ϕ0=0.4 and feedback adoption, with nominal 95% tG−1 intervals and the G/(G−1) factor. With G=100 clusters of 5 units, the biases of τ̂, κ̂ and ϕ̂ were 0.0009 (MCSE 0.0023), 0.0006 (0.0032) and 0.0021 (0.0021); the empirical standard deviations were 0.0733, 0.1025 and 0.0668 against mean standard errors of 0.0741, 0.1022 and 0.0674; and coverage was 0.967 (0.0056), 0.955 (0.0066) and 0.953 (0.0067). With G=50 clusters of 10 units, the biases were 0.0015 (0.0023), −0.0028 (0.0032) and 0.0011 (0.0022); the empirical standard deviations 0.0740, 0.1010 and 0.0690 against mean standard errors of 0.0723, 0.0998 and 0.0673; and coverage 0.952 (0.0068), 0.957 (0.0064) and 0.947 (0.0071). In both designs the correlation between τ̂−τ0 and its linearisation was 0.9998.

For Theorem 3(a),(c), with N=2000, T=10, k=10, R=200 and τ0=log0.8, the two-step log-R estimator (c=0.5) had bias −0.2310 (MCSE 0.0007) under feedback adoption, composed of a small-count part BJ=−0.0334 and a feedback part BF=−0.1976, and bias 0.0071 (0.0008) under random adoption, with BJ=0.0088 and BF=−0.0017; the decomposition identity held to machine precision. Two-way fixed effects on log(Y+1) had bias 0.6989 (0.0025) under feedback adoption, of which 0.9687 is the contribution of the omitted log infection pressure, and −0.1366 (0.0040) under random adoption, with an omitted-pressure contribution of −0.1573.

For Lemma 2 (G=40 clusters of 5 units, T=8, 4000 replications), cumulative cases of neighbouring clusters were correlated (0.0771 under feedback adoption, MCSE 0.0022), but the cross-cluster products of moment contributions had mean zero. The largest |z|-statistic for the policy rows was 0.311. The ratio of the Monte Carlo variance of Gĝ(θ0) to the mean of Ω̂ lay in [0.9694,1.0264] under feedback adoption. The lead moment of Proposition 2(c) had z=−214.48 under feedback adoption and z=−1.12 under random adoption. For T=2 and τ0=−0.2231, solving (6) numerically gave the Poisson fixed-effects pseudo-true values −0.5240 under threshold adoption (bias −0.3009) and −0.2272 under random adoption (bias −0.004). Simulation means over 20×200,000 units were −0.5233 and −0.2266 (MCSE 0.0004). For Theorem 4(a), the cumulative relative difference between 𝔼ν and 𝔼Y(0) was 0.00229 (largest weekly |z|=1.86), against −0.8449 for naive rescaling.
